examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Normal forms are defined relative to all implied dependencies and candidate keys. Prime attributes occur in some candidate key. BCNF requires every nontrivial FD determinant to be a superkey; 3NF alternatively permits a prime dependent attribute. Thus 3NF can hold without BCNF. Partial dependencies and transitive dependencies require careful key context, rather than merely spotting a two-attribute left side.

**Key relationship:** BCNF: every nontrivial FD determinant is a superkey

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Find all candidate keys and prime attributes.
2. Check every relevant nontrivial FD.
3. Use determinant superkey and dependent-prime tests.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Identify all candidate keys and prime attributes first. BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. 3NF also permits a prime attribute on the right. 2NF forbids a nonprime attribute depending on a proper subset of any candidate key. Atomic values establish 1NF, not higher forms.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
R(A,B,C) has A→B and B→C, with A its only candidate key. How many listed dependencies violate BCNF?

**Answer: 1.** A→B has a superkey determinant and is allowed. B→C has a determinant B whose closure is {B,C}, missing A, so it violates BCNF. Exactly one listed dependency violates it; it also violates 3NF because C is nonprime.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
A relation can have several candidate keys. Checking only the designated primary key can miss partial dependencies or prime-attribute exceptions.

3NF permits a non-superkey determinant when the dependent attribute is prime; BCNF does not.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

BCNF requires for each nontrivial X→A:

- **A.** X contains one attribute
- **B.** A never repeats
- **C.** A is always prime
- **D.** X is a superkey

**Answer: D.** BCNF's determinant condition is that X determines the whole relation.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** BCNF implies 3NF
- **B.** 3NF always implies BCNF
- **C.** Prime attributes belong to some candidate key
- **D.** Normal-form testing depends on dependencies, not just a sample

**Answer: A, C, D.** 3NF permits some non-superkey determinants when the dependent attribute is prime, so it is weaker.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

R(A,B,C), F={A→B,B→A}. How many candidate keys?



**Answer: 2.** C must be included because no FD derives it. AC and BC each determine all attributes and are minimal; no other minimal keys exist.

examGuide.title: Work through the supplied PYQs
examGuide.body:
#### GATE 2024 CS1 · Q22 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/normal-forms?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Normal forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. 1NF requires atomic attribute values; a composite attribute must be broken into its components in the relational schema. C is true.
2. Atomicity does not prevent a key from containing several separate attributes, so A is true.
3. Foreign keys and multiple candidate keys are allowed in 1NF, making B and D false. Select **A,C**.

#### GATE 2025 CS2 · Q46 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/normal-forms?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Normal forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. In R1, A and D never appear on a right side, so every key includes both; AD determines all attributes and is the only candidate key. D→E has a nonsuperkey determinant and nonprime right side, violating 3NF. C is true.
2. In R2, C is the only candidate key: C→A→B,D. A alone cannot determine C, so A→B and A→D violate 3NF with nonprime right sides. D is true.
3. Select **C,D**; A,B are false.
